Asian Dairy Milk and Food Company, (A Proprietorship Concern of Mr. Ajay Gupta) Having office and residence at: D-1135, Gali No.7, Ashok Nagar, Wazirabad Road, Delhi-110093. .....Accused Offence Complained of or proved : U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 Plea of the Accused : Pleaded not guilty Date of filing : 08.09.2016 Date of Institution : 14.09.2016 Date of reserving judgment/order : 11.11.2025 Final Order/Judgment : Conviction Date of pronouncement : 23.12.2025 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this Judgment, I shall decide the present complaint filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 by the complainant against the accused. Factual Matrix 2. Briefly stated, the case of the complainant is that the accused proprietorship approached the complainant seeking financial assistance to AKANKSHA SINGH CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 3 of 24 Digitally signed by AKANKSHA SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:46:41 +0530 meet its financial requirements in respect of its business. The complainant, at request, sanctioned credit facilities to the accused to the tunes of Rs. 1,25,00,000/- as cash credit limit and Bank guarantee limit of Rs. 2,00,00,000/- as original credit facilities. At request of the accused, these facilities were renewed and enhanced vide sanction letter dated 27.05.2013 wherein the cash credit facility was enhanced to Rs. 2,00,00,000/- and the bank guarantee facility was reduced to Rs. 1,25,00,000/-. Thereafter vide sanction letter dated 25.10.2013, these facilities were again renewed and enhanced and the cash credit facility was enhanced to Rs. 4,00,00,000/- and the bank guarantee limit was reduced to Rs. 1,00,00,000/-. Again, vide sanction letter dated 06.12.2014, the cash credit was enhanced to Rs. 4,50,00,000/- by converting a portion of the bank guarantee limit of Rs. 50,00,000/- to cash credit and the balance of Rs. 50,00,000/- remained as bank guarantee. In 2015, at the request of the accused, the cash credit limit was renewed and the bank guarantee limit remained unchanged. 3. The accused failed to make the payment of the amount due and accrued in the credit facilities as per the terms and conditions of the loan documents and the complainant classified the account of the accused as NPA in April, 2016. As on 31.05.2016, a sum of Rs. 4,67,02,254.88/-, together with interest was due and payable by the accused to the complainant. 4. Against the said dues, and in partial discharge of his legally enforceable liability, the accused issued one cheque bearing no. 905333 dated 03.08.2016, drawn on RBL Bank, Barakhamba Road for a sum of Rs. 3,25,00,000/-. However, when the said cheque was presented by the complainant to his bank within the jurisdiction of this court, the same was AKANKSHA SINGH CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 4 of 24 Digitally signed by AKANKSHA SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:46:48 +0530 returned dishonoured with remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide cheque return memo dated 08.08.2016. Thereafter, the complainant issued a legal demand notice dated 10.08.2016 upon the accused demanding payment. Since no repayment was made by the accused within stipulated 15 days from date of receipt of legal demand notice, hence the present complaint was filed U/s. 138 NI Act . Proceedings Before the Court 5. Upon consideration of pre-summoning evidence, cognizance of offence under Section 138 NI Act was taken and the accused was summoned. Thereafter, on 19.01.2023, separate notice explaining the accusation was put to the accused under Section 251 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as ' CrPC ') to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 6. At this stage the accused admitted the signatures on the cheque but denied filling up its material particulars. He admitted that he had taken cash credit facility from the complainant bank, in lieu of which 4 blank signed cheques were taken by the complainant. He stated that in November, 2022, he came to know that the bank had already sold his property off and as such, he claimed that there was no remaining liability. The accused denied the receipt of the legal demand notice as well as the address on the said notice. 7. In support of his case, the AR of the Complainant deposed as CW-1 and he relied on his post-summoning evidence and further relied upon the documents namely the power of attorney, Ex. CW1/1, authority letter of the previous AR Ex. CW1/A, original cheque in question with the bank return memo, i.e. Ex. CW1/B (Colly) and the legal demand notice dated Digitally signed by AKANKSHA CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 5 of 24 AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:46:55 +0530 10.08.2016 alongwith postal receipts, i.e. Ex. CW1/C (Colly). In her evidentiary affidavit, the AR of the complainant reiterated the contents of her complaint. Further, the cross examination of CW1 was conducted wherein the following notable points emerged: 7.1. CW1 admitted that he had not filed on record the documents which were taken from the accused at the time of giving the cash credit/bank guarantee. He stated that he did not remember if at the time of taking the cash credit/bank guarantee by the accused, the valuation of the property was done or not. 7.2. He admitted that generally the employee or concerned person visits the property for valuation but stated that he did not remember who visited the mortgaged property at the time of valuation. 7.3. He stated that the mortgaged property was auctioned by the complainant under SARFAESI Act for approximately Rs. 2.89 Crores. He stated that the bank has issued the sales certificate to the auction purchaser but admitted that the same has not been filed on record. 7.4. He stated that he was not aware as to how much amount the complainant bank has received from the accused during the tenure of the loan and that the same can be confirmed only from the records. He admitted that the complainant bank had not produced the statement of account of the accused for the tenure 2012 to 2016. 7.5. He admitted that no documentary proof had been placed on record to show that the accused had made request to change the CC limit of his account. He stated that he was not aware of such request was Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 6 of 24 2025.12.23 17:47:02 +0530 made orally or in writing and the same has to be verified from records. 7.6. He stated that the legal demand notice was sent to the accused on the address of the mortgaged property, but he could not tell when the bank took the possession of the mortgaged property. He denied the suggestion that at the time when the legal notice was sent by the complainant bank, the possession of the mortgaged property had already been taken by the complainant bank. 7.7. He denied the suggestion that since in the year 2012, the initial sanction was of Rs. 3,25,00,000/-, the cheque in question was taken from the accused before the sanction of the loan for the said amount. 7.8. He stated that he was not aware as to how much payment was received from the accused before declaring the account of the accused as NPA or if any payment was received from the accused after his account was declared as NPA on 30.04.2016. 7.9. He admitted that no board resolution was placed on record in support of his power of attorney. 7.10. He denied any knowledge of any FIR u/s 420 IPC against certain employees of the bank. 7.11. CW-1 brought on record the sanction letter dated 19.07.2012, i.e. Mark S, the statement of account of accused from 2012 to 2017, i.e. Mark T and the possession notice, i.e. Mark U. 7.12. He stated that at the time of sanctioning of loan, the bank generally takes audited financial statements, existing bank statements, net worth letter etc., but stated that he could not tell what specific documents were taken from the accused without seeing the records. Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 7 of 24 SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:47:09 +0530 7.13. He stated that only one cheque has been taken from the accused, qua which the present complaint has been filed and that it was taken in August,2016. 7.14. He admitted that he had not brought the valuation report of the property that was made prior to the sanction of loan. 7.15. He stated that he will have to check if approximately the amount of Rs. 2 Crores was given to the complainant on account of interest by the accused. 7.16. He stated that as per the possession letter Mark U, the physical possession of the property was taken by the complainant bank on 22.11.2016. Thereafter, CE was closed. 8. All the incriminating evidence was put before the accused and the statement of accused u/s 313 Cr.PC was recorded. The accused reiterated and elaborated on the defence disclosed by him at the stage of framing of notice under Section 251 CrPC. He stated that the complainant bank had approached him for opening a branch at his property, but later stated after deliberating for 3-4 months that the same could not be done as the property did not have MCD approved Naksha. Thereafter, the representative of the complainant advised him to open a bank account in their bank and stated that credit facilities would be extended. He stated that the complainant never contacted him before enhancing or decreasing the credit limit or bank guarantee limit and he only got to know regarding the same way by way of text message from the complainant bank. Thereafter, he said he contacted his relationship manager who made him believe that the same was for his benefit only. The accused further stated that the representative of the complainant bank approached his wife CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 8 of 24 AKANKSHA SINGH Digitally signed by AKANKSHA SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:47:17 +0530 behind his back and took 4-5 blank signed cheques and around 5-6 blank letter pads from his home and misused the same. He stated that after utilising his credit limit to some extent, he approached the complainant bank and offered to sell the mortgaged property to his relative to repay the amount, but the representative of the complainant, i.e. Jitender Verma refused his offer as he wanted to make some illegal gains from his property. The accused further stated that his mortgaged property was of worth somewhere around Rs. 12 crores to Rs. 13 crores at the time but the complainant sold the said property for massive undervaluation of Rs. 2,50,00,000/-, as he got to know through other people. 9. In his statement u/s 313 CrPC, the accused also stated that as per his information, around Rs. 5 Crores were taken from the buyer under the table. He stated that he was never given any notice by the complainant bank regarding possession of the mortgaged property and since he was not residing at the said property, he never got to know that when the bank took possession of his property. He stated that the cheque in question is one of the 4-5 blank signed cheques taken by the representative of the complainant from his wife in his absence. He denied the receipt of the legal demand notice. The accused opted to lead DE. 10.However, on the NDOH, ld. Counsel for the accused submitted that the accused did not wish to lead DE. Accordingly, the Defence Evidence was closed and final arguments were heard from both the parties. During the course of final arguments, ld. Counsel for the complainant submitted that: 10.1. The accused has admitted the signatures on the cheque in question as well as the fact that a cash credit and bank guarantee facility was extended to him. He has also admitted that his property was Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 9 of 24 SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:47:26 +0530 mortgaged with the complainant bank and the sole defence that the accused has brought forth is that after sale of his mortgaged property, no liability remains. 10.2. In the cross-examination of CW-1, the personal guarantee given by the accused as well as the bank guarantee remain unchallenged. The statement of account Mark T also shows that the outstanding amount is of Rs. 4.67 Crores. 10.3. The Hon'ble DRT has already decided the case qua the loan in question, wherein relief has been granted in favour of the complainant. The judgment of DRT shows at page no. 10 that the complainant bank had duly sent a legal demand notice dated 10.08.2016 to the accused u/s 13(2) SARFAESI Act, to which the accused sent objections. This shows that the accused was well aware of the proceedings. 10.4. The argument that the bank had physical possession of the mortgaged property on the date of legal notice is false. On 24.08.2016, the complainant bank had only taken symbolic possession of the mortgaged property as per Section 13(4) of SARFAESI Act. Infact, the complainant bank has obtained physical possession only 3 months after the date of the legal notice. 10.5. Even if the defence of the accused that the cheque in question was given as a mere security cheque is accepted, the same does not hold good unless the accused can prove that he did not have a legally enforceable liability qua the cheque amount. The accused has nowhere been able to establish that. 10.6. The accused submits that after the sale of mortgaged property, all dues are settled. However, as per the statement of account, Mark T, AKANKSHA SINGH Digitally signed by CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 10 of 24 AKANKSHA SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:47:33 +0530 even after the settlement of money obtained by way of sale of mortgaged property, the liability of the accused remains. 10.7. So far as the sale of the mortgaged property is concerned, the accused has duly accepted that there were 8 shops in the said mortgaged property. The accused had already sold these 8 shops to the purchasers, after taking the credit facility. After the complainant bank took possession of the mortgaged property, the said shopowners filed an application with the DRT, which was dismissed. In appeal before the Hon'ble DRAT, the said shopowners settled the matter with the complainant bank, paid Rs. 2.89 Crores and took possession of the property. After appropriation of the sale amount as well, the remaining liability of the accused is approximately over Rs. 4 Crores. 10.8. The valuation of the property cannot be decided by the present court and the correct remedy for the accused would have been under SARFAESI Act , which he has failed to take. Infact, the accused has not even challenged the recovery order passed by the Hon'ble DRT. 10.9. Even if the accused had not approved the enhancement of the cash credit limit, the accused was well within its rights to not use the enhanced cash credit limit. However, the accused used the said limit without any complaint and only raised an issue when the amount was demanded back from him. 11.Per Contra, Ld. Counsel for the accused prayed that the accused be acquitted. The points raised by ld. Counsel for the accused during his final arguments are as follows: Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:47:40 +0530 CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 11 of 24 11.1. The complainant has failed to produce the valuation report of the property, which was of Rs. 6 Crores approximately at the time of taking the bank guarantee and cash credit facility. Despite putting questions to the AR of the complainant several times, the complainant did not bring forward the valuation report as it would have shown that even on the date of mortgage, the value of the property was more than Rs. 6 Crores. 11.2. The cash credit facility of the bank was changed on its own without consulting the accused. No letter of request for any such change sent by the accused has been placed on record. Infact, in the year 2015, the accused also made representation to the bank requesting and asking why changes had been made without asking or informing him. 11.3. The cheque in question was one of the security cheques given by the accused at the time of taking the initial credit facility on 09.07.2012. At the time, the accused was also told to open a savings account in the same bank and the cheque in question pertains to the same account in the same bank. The complainant bank was very well aware that there was no sufficient balance in the saving account of the accused and as such it is implausible that they would accept the cheque of Rs. 3.25 Crores as repayment of the dues. 11.4. On 31.05.2016, as per the statement of account of the complainant itself the total liability of the accused was of Rs. 4.67 Crores. No justification has been provided as to why the cheque has been accepted for a lesser amount when the entire loan account is NPA. CW-1 merely states that it was in part fulfilment of the liability, but Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 12 of 24 17:47:46 +0530 the cheque in question does not even mention the loan account number. The sole reason that the cheque is for Rs. 3.25 Crores is because initially when the cash credit facility was taken in 2012, the total amount of the same was Rs. 3.25 Crores and the present cheque was a security cheque qua the same. 11.5. The legal notice had never been delivered to the accused. Even the tracking report annexed with the complaint shows that the same has been delivered only to Nand Nagri "SO" i.e. the Sorting Office, and not to the addressee at his address in Wazirabad. 11.6. In 2012, the value of the property of the accused was around Rs. 6 Crores and in the year 2020, it must have been atleast around Rs. 10-12 Crores but the complainant has intentionally sold it for a much lesser amount than even the initial loan amount of Rs. 3.25 crores. The complainant has also not filed the sales certificate qua the mortgaged property. 11.7. The testimony of CW-1 is not to be read in evidence as he admits that he had joined the bank only in May, 2018 and had no knowledge of Cash credit or bank guarantee facility qua the present complaint. CW-1 has also not placed on record the board resolution qua his power of attorney document. 11.8. As per the SOA of the bank itself, Rs. 1.93 Crores have already been paid by the accused to the bank. The same was paid by the accused as repayment of the loan amount only but the complainant kept adjusting it against the interest amount. 11.9. The property was in the possession of the bank when the legal notice was delivered. Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:47:54 +0530 CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 13 of 24 12.I have heard the counsels for both the parties, considered the evidence led by them carefully and have perused the court records thoroughly. 13. Before going into the facts of the present case, it would be apposite to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both sides. In order to establish the offence under Section 138 of NI Act, the complainant must fulfil all the essential ingredients of the offence as laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Gimpex Private Limited vs. Manoj Goel (2022) 11 SCC 705, as highlighted below: "1st Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by a person on an account maintained by him/her for payment of money and the same is presented for payment within a period of 3 months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity; 2nd Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by the drawer for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability; 3rd Ingredient: The cheque was returned unpaid by the bank due to either insufficiency of funds in the account to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account on an agreement made with that bank; 4th Ingredient: A demand of the said amount has been made by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque by a notice in writing given to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information of the dishonour of cheque from the bank; Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:48:02 +0530 CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 14 of 24 5th Ingredient: The drawer fails to make payment of the said amount of money within fifteen days from the date of receipt of notice." 14. The cheque herein was dated 03.08.2016 and was dishonoured vide return memo dated 08.08.2016. Thereafter, the complainant sent a legal demand notice dated 10.08.2016 to the accused demanding to make payment of the cheque amount. Upon non-payment, the present case was filed. Prima facie, therefore, it appears that the complaint is well within the period of limitation and the prescribed period for procedure u/s 138 has been duly complied with. 15.So far as the ingredients aforesaid are concerned, the accused has admitted the signature on the cheque in question. The complainant has proved the original cheque (Ex. CW1/B), which the accused has not disputed as being drawn on his account. It is not disputed that the cheque in question was presented within the validity period. Further, the cheque in question was returned unpaid vide return memo (Ex. CW1/B) due to the reason, "funds insufficient", which falls strictly within the purview of section 138 NI Act. As such, on the basis of the above, the first and third ingredients of the offence under Section 138 NI Act stand proved. 16.So far as the fourth and fifth ingredients are concerned, the accused has denied the receipt of the legal notice at every stage. The accused has stated that on the date of the legal notice, the property was in the possession of the bank. However, the possession letter Mark U shows that the possession of the property was taken by the complainant bank on 22.11.2016 while the legal notice was duly sent on 11.08.2016 and was delivered on 12.08.2016. Nothing has been placed on record to show that the accused was not residing on the said address at the relevant period. Digitally signed by CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 15 of 24 AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:48:10 +0530 However, even if the accused was not residing at that address on the date of delivery of legal notice, the complainant bank has duly sent the legal demand notice on the last known correct address of the accused, as per its records. 17.Moreover, as per mandate of C.C. Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed & Anr. (2007) 6 SCC 555, the accused didn't make the payment within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the Court and thus he cannot contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 . When the notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing the drawer of the cheque, the mandatory requirement of issue of notice in terms of Clause (b) of proviso to Section 138 of the Act stands complied with. As such, the fourth and fifth ingredients also stand proved. 18.In the light of the defence put forth by the accused, the decision of this case is dependent on the determination of the sole issue, i.e. Whether the cheque in question was issued to discharge a legally recoverable debt. 19.The accused, at the stage of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC as well as, in his statement under Section 313, has admitted that the cheque in question was signed by him. As such, the presumptions under Section 118 and 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act come into effect and it is presumed that the cheque in question was drawn for consideration and that the cheque had been given to the holder in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. 20.Before delving into the defence of the accused, it is imperative to discuss the law regarding the standard of proof required to discharge the burden of presumption under Section 139 NI Act. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 16 of 24 Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:48:18 +0530 in the case of Rajesh Jain v. Ajay Singh 2021 SCC OnLine SC 1275 has discussed the law on this point in detail, stating: "40. The standard of proof to discharge this evidential burden is not as heavy as that usually seen in situations where the prosecution is required to prove the guilt of an accused. The accused is not expected to prove the non-existence of the presumed fact beyond reasonable doubt. The accused must meet the standard of 'preponderance of probabilities', similar to a defendant in a civil proceeding. 41. In order to rebut the presumption and prove to the contrary, it is open to the accused to raise a probable defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested. The words 'until the contrary is proved' occurring in Section 139 do not mean that accused must necessarily prove the negative that the instrument is not issued in discharge of any debt/liability but the accused has the option to ask the Court to consider the non-existence of debt/liability so probable that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the case, to act upon the supposition that debt/liability did not exist. 42. In other words, the accused is left with two options. The first option-of proving that the debt/liability does not exist-is to lead defence evidence and conclusively establish with certainty that the cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt/liability. The second option is to prove the non-existence of debt/liability by a preponderance of probabilities by referring to the particular circumstances of the case. The preponderance of probability in favour of the accused's Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 17 of 24 SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:48:25 +0530 case may be even fifty one to forty nine and arising out of the entire circumstances of the case, which includes: the complainant's version in the original complaint, the case in the legal/demand notice, complainant's case at the trial, as also the plea of the accused in the reply notice, his 313 statement or at the trial as to the circumstances under which the promissory note/cheque was executed. All of them can raise a preponderance of probabilities justifying a finding that there was 'no debt/liability'" 21.Thus, it is established position of law that to rebut the presumption under Section 139 NI Act, the standard of proof is that of preponderance of probabilities and that the accused may rely on circumstantial evidence to prove the same. The preponderance of probabilities must be adjudged on the basis of the complainant's case as well as the defence of the accused. 22. The accused has not disputed the cash credit and bank guarantee facility taken initially and has solely disputed the subsequent enhancements. The signatures on the cheques, as well as the amount of credit facility utilised, have not been disputed. 23.One of the arguments raised by Ld. Counsel for the accused is that the cheque in question was given as a security cheque at the time of the initial agreement and as such, no liability exists. Under Section 138 NI Act, the averment that a blank signed security cheque has been misused is no defence unless the accused can prove on a scale of preponderance of probabilities that he did not have a crystallized legal liability co-extensive to the cheque amount on the date of presentation of the cheque. Reliance can be placed on Bir Singh v Mukesh Kumar (2019) 4 SCC 197 & Digitally CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 18 of 24 signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:48:32 +0530 Credential Leasing & Credits Ltd. v Shruti Investment 2015 SCC OnLine Del 10061. 24.The Hon'ble apex court in Sripati Singh v. State of Jharkhand 2021 SCC Online SC 1002 has observed that: "Further, the borrower would have the option of repaying the loan amount or such financial liability in any other form and in that manner if the amount of loan due and payable has been discharged within the agreed period, the cheque issued as security cannot thereafter be presented. Therefore, the prior discharge of the loan or there being an altered situation due to which there would be understanding between the parties is a sine qua non to not present the cheque which was issued as security. These are only the defences that would be available to the drawer of the cheque in a proceedings initiated under Section 138 of the N.I. Act." Thus, if the accused is able to prove that there was no legally recoverable debt or that the amount has already been repaid or that there has been an altered situation, the defence of security cheque becomes a valid defence. This defence, thus, has to be analysed in the light of the other defences. 25.Even so, this defence as to security cheques has also not been consistent inasmuch as in his statement u/s 313 CrPC, the accused has stated that the cheque in question was one of the blank signed cheques taken by the representative of the complainant from his wife behind his back. In the said statement, the accused nowhere stated that the said cheques were given by him as blank signed security cheques at the time of availing the credit facility. Digitally signed by AKANKSHA AKANKSHA SINGH CNR no.DLND02-017673-2016 RBL Bank Ltd. Vs. Asian Dairy & Ors. Page No. 19 of 24 SINGH Date: 2025.12.23 17:48:40 +0530 26. The accused has not led Defence Evidence but in his statement u/s 313, he has put forth his detailed defence. Even as per the said defence, the accused does not dispute factum of loan and merely states that the bank has sold his property for a much lesser value than the original value of the property and that is why he does not owe any liability. The fact remains admitted that the property in question has been sold by the complainant bank after the date of the presentation of the cheque in question. Thus, even if the assertion that the property was sold for an undervaluation is true, that does not change the fact that the accused had in fact taken the cash credit facility and as on date of presentment of the cheque in question, there was an existing legally enforceable liability of the cheque amount. Thus, the fact that the initial valuation report or the sale certificate has not been brought on record is of no relevance at this stage. 27.So far as the enhancement of cash credit limit without consent is concerned, the accused could very well have not utilised the extended credit limit even if the same was extended without consent. However, after utilising the said amount, the accused can no longer use the defence that there was no consent taken from him especially when he has admitted that he had received a message from the complainant bank regarding the enhancement of the same. 28.Another defence put forth by Ld. Counsel for the accused is that no justification has been provided by the complainant as to why the cheque has been accepted for a lesser amount when the entire liability is of Rs. 4.67 Crores. However, this is not a case when the cheque amount is more than the liability, but is infact quite the opposite. The complainant is under no obligation to provide a justification especially when no other plausible defence has been put forth by the accused. Reference in this regard may be made to the observations of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Naresh Potteries vs. Aarti Industries (2025) 1 S.C.R. 41: "21. It could thus be seen that this Court distinguished the position of a complainant filing a complaint on behalf of an individual from the position of a complainant filing a complaint on behalf of a company. This Court clarified that although the decision in the case of A.C. Narayanan (supra) had taken centre stage, the facts involved in that case were in the background that the complaint filed was based on the power of attorney issued by the 'payee' who was also an individual. In such cases, the manner in which the power was being exercised had to be explicitly stated. However, this Court clarified that the position that would emerge when the complainant is a company or a corporate entity will have to be viewed from a different standpoint. Ajay Singh (supra) , I have considered the complainant's version in the original complaint, the case in the legal notice, complainant's case at the trial, the statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC as to the circumstances under which the cheque was executed. Having considered all the above it is clear that the defence of the accused is based on a bare denial of the averments made in the complaint and that the defence raised by the accused has not been proved at any stage, nor has the accused been able to prove the non-existence of debt/liability by a preponderance of probabilities by referring to the particular circumstances of this case.
